items.zh: 云何七種苦？謂生苦、老苦、病苦、死苦、怨憎會苦、愛別離苦、求不得苦。
items.en: What are the seven kinds of suffering? The suffering of birth, the suffering of old age, the suffering of illness, the suffering of death, the suffering of encountering what one resents, the suffering of separation from what one loves, and the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks.

items.zh: 云何七種慢？謂慢、過慢、慢過慢、我慢、增上慢、卑慢、邪慢。
items.en: What are the seven kinds of conceit? Conceit, excessive conceit, conceit beyond excessive conceit, self-conceit, overestimating conceit, self-deprecating conceit, and wrong conceit.

items.zh: 云何七種憍？謂無病憍、少年憍、長壽憍、族姓憍、色力憍、富貴憍、多聞憍。
items.en: What are the seven kinds of arrogance? Arrogance over good health, arrogance over youth, arrogance over long life, arrogance over lineage, arrogance over physical beauty and strength, arrogance over wealth and rank, and arrogance over learning.

items.title: Four Kinds of Speech: Seeing, Hearing, Reflection, Direct Knowledge

items.zh: 云何四種言說？謂依見、聞、覺、知所有言說。依見言說者，謂依眼故，現見外色，由此因緣，為他宣說，是名依見言說。依聞言說者，謂從他聞，由此因緣，為他宣說，是名依聞言說。
items.en: What are the four kinds of speech? Speech based on seeing, on hearing, on reflection, and on direct knowledge. Speech based on seeing is speech that, in dependence on the eye, actually perceives external form, and on that basis is spoken to others. Speech based on hearing is speech that, having been heard from another, is on that basis spoken to others.

items.zh: 依覺言說者，謂不見不聞，但自思惟、稱量、觀察，由此因緣，為他宣說，是名依覺言說。依知言說者，謂各別於內、所受、所證、所觸、所得，由此因緣，為他宣說，是名依知言說。
items.en: Speech based on reflection is speech that, without having seen or heard something directly, arises simply from one's own reflection, estimation, and observation, and is on that basis spoken to others. Speech based on direct knowledge is speech concerning what one has individually felt, realised, experienced, and attained within oneself, spoken to others on that basis.

items.title: Many Kinds of Speech-Terms: A Full Taxonomy of Language

items.zh: 云何眾多言說句？謂即此亦名釋詞句，亦名戲論句，亦名攝義句，如是等類，眾多差別。又諸字母能攝諸義，當知亦名眾多言說句。
items.en: What are the many kinds of speech-terms? These same terms are also called explanatory terms, terms of elaboration, and meaning-comprehending terms, along with other such distinctions. The very letters of the alphabet, which comprehend all meanings, should likewise be understood as belonging among these many kinds of speech-terms.

items.zh: 彼復云何？所謂地、根、境、法、補特伽羅、自性、差別、作用、自、他、有、無、問、答、取、與、正性、邪性句。又有聽制、功德、過失、得、不得、毀、譽、苦、樂、稱、譏、堅妙、智退、沈、量、助伴、示現、教導、讚勵、慶慰句。又有七言論句，此即七例句。
items.en: What, then, are these terms? They include: ground, faculty, object, dharma, person, own-nature, distinction, function, self, other, existence, non-existence, question, answer, taking, giving, right nature, and wrong nature. There are, further, terms of what is permitted and prohibited, merit, fault, gain, loss, disparagement and praise spoken behind one's back, suffering, pleasure, praise and mockery spoken to one's face, firm excellence, the decline of wisdom, dullness, restlessness, accompaniment, manifestation, instruction, encouragement, and rejoicing. There are, further, the seven terms of grammatical case — the seven classical declensions.

items.zh: 謂補盧沙、補盧衫、補盧崽拏、補盧沙耶、補盧沙䫂、補盧殺娑、補盧鎩，如是等。復

有施設、教勅、標相、靜息、表了、軌則、安立、積集、決定、配屬、驚駭、初、中、後句。族姓等、立宗、言說、成辦、受用、尋求、守護、羞恥、憐愍、堪忍、怖畏、簡擇句。又有父母妻子等，一切所攝資具，應當廣說。及生老等，乃至所求不得、愁歎、少年、無病、長壽、愛會、怨離、所欲隨應、若不隨應，往來、顧視、若屈若申、行住坐臥、警悟、語默、解睡、解勞句。又有飲噉、咀味、串習、不串習、放逸、不放逸、廣略、增減、尋伺、煩惱、隨煩惱、戲論、離戲論、力劣、所成、能成、流轉、定異、相應、勢速、次第、時、方、數、和合、不和合、相似、不相似句。又有雜糅、共有、現見、不現見、隱顯句。又有能作、所作、法律、世事、資產、真妄、利益、非利益、骨體、疑慮、驚怪句。又有怯弱、無畏、顯了、不顯了、殺害、繫縛、禁閉、割截、驅擯句。又有罵詈、忿怒、捶打、迫脅、訶責、燒爛、燥暑、摧伏、渾濁、聖教隨逐比度句。
items.en: There are, further, terms of designation, decree, distinguishing mark, quiescence, expression, rule, establishment, accumulation, determination, correlation, alarm, and beginning, middle, and end. There are terms of lineage, the setting forth of a thesis, statement, accomplishment, enjoyment, seeking, protection, shame, compassion, forbearance, fear, and discernment. There are terms covering parents, spouse and children, and every kind of household requisite, treated at length; and terms of birth, old age, and on through unfulfilled longing, sorrow and lament, youth, health, long life, meeting with the loved, and parting from the hated. There are terms of eating and tasting, habituation and its absence, heedlessness and heedfulness, investigation and analysis, affliction and its secondary forms, and elaboration. There are terms of mixture, commonality, the seen and the unseen, and the hidden and manifest. There are terms of agent and action, law, worldly affairs, property, truth and falsehood, and benefit and harm. There are terms of timidity, fearlessness, killing, binding, confinement, mutilation, and expulsion. And there are terms of cursing, fury, beating, coercion, and reproach.

blocks.text: The last reading of fascicle 2 finishes the lists with three that bear directly on practice (suffering, conceit, and arrogance) and then two on language: four kinds of speech, and a long catalogue of "speech-terms", the ordinary words by which we name things. It is a shorter day; use the extra time to review the seven conceits, which recur throughout Buddhist psychology.
One passage is untranslated (0289c01–c03): a list of Sanskrit grammatical forms of the word *puruṣa*, "person" (補盧沙、補盧衫…), given as an example of how one word is inflected.

The usual list of sufferings has eight: birth, ageing, sickness, death, separation from the loved, meeting the disliked, not getting what one wants, and the five aggregates of clinging. Here only seven are given; the last is missing. Venerable Miào Jìng, citing the *Pīxún jì*, explains why: these seven are felt by everyone, Buddhist or not, so they are easy to understand. The suffering of the five aggregates is subtler; it is the suffering of conditioned formations we met on Day 7.
**Conceit** (慢, *māna*) is the mind's habit of measuring itself against others. The seven kinds:

items: **Conceit** (慢): thinking oneself superior to an inferior, or equal to an equal.
**Excessive conceit** (過慢): thinking oneself superior to an equal, or equal to a superior.

**Conceit beyond excessive conceit** (慢過慢): thinking oneself superior to one who is in fact superior. Venerable Miào Jìng: "in fact the other person's level is above mine, but I think I am above his."
**Self-conceit** (我慢): pride based on the view of a self.
**Overestimating conceit** (增上慢): claiming an attainment one has not reached. (We met this on Lamrim Day 1 as well.)
**Self-deprecating conceit** (卑慢): thinking oneself only a little inferior to one far superior.
**Wrong conceit** (邪慢): pride in what has no worth at all.

blocks.text: Notice that the first kind includes judging oneself *equal* to an equal. It may be accurate; it is still conceit, because the mind is busy measuring.

**Arrogance** (憍, *mada*) is pride in what one has: health, youth, long life, lineage, beauty and strength, wealth and rank, and learning. Venerable Miào Jìng's distinction is clear and useful: "Conceit is clinging centred on the self; arrogance is clinging centred on what is mine." Conceit compares; arrogance is intoxicated with possessions.

Speech based on seeing, on hearing, on reflection, and on direct knowledge. "Speech based on reflection" (依覺言說) is speech that, without having seen or heard, arises from one's own estimation and observation and is then told to others. Note that 覺 here is reflection or inference, not awakening. Speech based on **direct knowledge** (依知言說) is speech from one's own inner experience.
This list is the root of the Buddhist rules about honest speech: say what you saw as seen, what you heard as heard, what you inferred as inferred, and what you know as known.

The fascicle ends with a long catalogue of words people use: names for persons, for places, for times, for qualities, for mental states. Venerable Miào Jìng glosses two of them: 沈 is dullness ("sitting there meaning to practise and dozing off") and 量 is the restless, discriminating mind ("that is restlessness, that is distraction").

Why does a treatise on yoga end a fascicle with a dictionary? Recall Day 7: the dominant cause of a life is "delight in elaboration", the linguistic seeds laid down by naming. This catalogue shows how vast that web of names is. Every term in it is a way the mental consciousness divides and labels experience, and every use of it perfumes a seed.

Fascicle 2 has moved from seeds and the embryo, through the formation and destruction of the world, to the ordinary furniture of human life: needs, speech, anger, pride. The thread is the same as in fascicle 1. The mental consciousness, through volition and naming, makes karma; karma, individual and shared, produces both the body and the world. Fascicle 3 completes the Mind Stage with the mental factors and the way the mind is organised.

quiz.q: The treatise lists seven kinds of suffering — one fewer than the usual eight. Which is missing, and why?
options: the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging is missing, because the seven are coarse and evident sufferings anyone can recognise, Buddhist or not, while the aggregates' suffering is subtler
the suffering of birth, because birth is joyful
the suffering of death, because after death there is no suffering
none is missing; the seven are the eight
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng, citing the *Pixunji*: "Because these seven sufferings are felt by anyone — not only Buddhists; non-Buddhists feel them too — they are easy to understand, so they are listed." Master Cháng Bǎi likewise says the seven are deliberately limited to what is "coarse and evident," reserving the subtler suffering inherent in the five aggregates for those who actually take up the practice. Venerable Miào Jìng adds: "If you do not cling … suffering is no longer suffering." B and C contradict the text — birth and death are both on the list.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT among the seven kinds of conceit listed in the treatise?
options: conceit beyond excessive conceit
overestimating conceit
self-deprecating conceit
arrogance over wealth and rank
quiz.why: The seven conceits are: conceit, excessive conceit, conceit beyond excessive conceit, self-conceit, overestimating conceit, self-deprecating conceit, and wrong conceit. D, "arrogance over wealth and rank," belongs to the seven arrogances of §60 — the list that immediately follows — testing whether conceit and arrogance are kept apart (see Q20-3 for the difference).

quiz.q: According to Venerable Miào Jìng, what is "conceit beyond excessive conceit"?
options: regarding oneself as superior to one who is inferior
regarding oneself as superior to an equal
regarding oneself as equal to one who is superior
regarding oneself as superior to one who is actually superior — the other person really surpasses me, yet I think I surpass him
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: "'Regarding oneself as superior to the superior' — in fact the other person's level is above mine, but I think I am above his; this is called 'conceit beyond excessive conceit.'" A is ordinary conceit (which also includes regarding oneself as equal to an equal); B and C together make up excessive conceit. Master Cháng Bǎi notes that all seven share one root — a mind that puffs itself up in comparison with others — which is why even genuine superiority can still count as conceit.

quiz.q: According to Venerable Miào Jìng, what is the basic difference between conceit (慢) and arrogance (憍)?
options: conceit is clinging centred on the self; arrogance is clinging centred on what is mine — what I possess
conceit concerns others, arrogance oneself
conceit is for monastics, arrogance for laypeople
there is no difference
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: "Conceit, above, is clinging centred on the self; arrogance is clinging centred on what is mine — what I possess." That is why all seven arrogances are "deep attachment and pride" in what one has: health, youth, long life, lineage, beauty and strength, wealth and rank, learning. Master Cháng Bǎi says each takes a temporary, conditional advantage for a permanent basis. Venerable Miào Jìng adds, citing the *Large Perfection of Wisdom*, that only from arhatship up is arrogance absent; what marks a noble one is noticing it the instant it arises and calming it.

quiz.q: Among the four kinds of speech, what is "speech based on reflection" (依覺言說)?
options: speech that perceives external form through the eye and is then spoken to others
speech that, without having seen or heard something directly, arises from one's own reflection, estimation, and observation, and is then spoken to others
speech heard from another and passed on
speech about what one has individually felt, realised, experienced, and attained
quiz.why: "Speech based on reflection is speech that, without having seen or heard something directly, arises simply from one's own reflection, estimation, and observation, and is on that basis spoken to others." A is speech based on seeing, C on hearing, and D on direct knowledge. The Chinese 覺 is easily misread as "sensation"; the translation's "reflection" captures its sense of inference — Master Cháng Bǎi calls it inferential speech. Venerable Miào Jìng adds that it is really the sixth consciousness that speaks — "the eye-consciousness cannot talk."

quiz.q: Among the many speech-terms are 沈 and 量 (translated "dullness, restlessness"). According to Venerable Miào Jìng, what do they refer to?
options: 沈 is heaviness, 量 is measurement
沈 is silence, 量 is magnanimity
沈 is sinking in water, 量 is quantity
沈 is dullness — dozing off when trying to practise; 量 is the mind's ceaseless discriminating and thinking — restlessness and distraction
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: "What is 沈? It is dullness — sitting there meaning to practise and dozing off; that is 沈. 量 is the mind discriminating and thinking — that is restlessness, that is distraction." The translation's "dullness, restlessness" agrees. A and C read the characters literally. In this passage he follows Master Kuījī's ten-fold grouping of the speech-terms, as does Master Cháng Bǎi.
